Augustine of Canterbury
AW-gus-teen uv KAN-ter-ber-ee
proper noun (a missionary; first Archbishop of Canterbury)
Named for Augustine (Latin Augustinus); the Benedictine monk sent by Gregory the Great to England in A.D. 597, not to be confused with Augustine of Hippo.

Biblical Definition

Augustine of Canterbury (died c. 604) was the Benedictine prior sent by Gregory the Great from Rome to the Anglo-Saxons of England in A.D. 597, becoming the first Archbishop of Canterbury and the leader of the mission that planted the Roman form of Christianity among the English. He is to be carefully distinguished from the far greater Augustine of Hippo. The dictionary honours what is honourable in his work: he obeyed the missionary impulse of the Great Commission—“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations”—and carried the name of Christ to a heathen people, baptizing King Ethelbert of Kent and many of his subjects, so that the gospel, however mixed, reached a pagan land. The labour of carrying glad tidings to those who had not heard is in itself a beautiful thing, for how shall they believe without a preacher. Yet the dictionary does not idealize him. The Christianity he planted was the developing Roman religion, with its sacramentalism, its veneration of relics and saints, and its submission to the papal see; and his dealings with the older Celtic British church were marked by a haughty insistence on Roman customs (the dating of Easter, the form of baptism, submission to himself) that bred division rather than unity. The dictionary applies its rule for non-Reformed figures: it honours the genuine missionary zeal that brought Christ's name to the English, while naming the Roman errors he carried with it. The conversion of England was a real mercy of God; the Roman dress in which it came was a corruption later generations, and at last the English Reformation, would have to strip away.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Benedictine monk sent by Gregory the Great to England in 597, first Archbishop of Canterbury (not Augustine of Hippo); honoured for the missionary zeal that brought Christ's name to the English, while the Roman errors he planted are named.

AUGUSTINE OF CANTERBURY, proper noun. The Benedictine monk sent by Gregory the Great to England, A.D. 597.

First Archbishop of Canterbury; not to be confused with Augustine of Hippo.

He obeyed the Great Commission, carrying Christ's name to the heathen Anglo-Saxons (Matthew 28:19).

He baptized King Ethelbert of Kent and many of his people.

Yet he planted the developing Roman religion and clashed haughtily with the Celtic British church.

Key Scripture

Mt 28:19 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:"

Ro 10:15 — "And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!"

Ac 1:8 — "But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth."

Ps 96:3 — "Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people."

Modern Corruption

Augustine of Canterbury carried the developing Roman religion—sacramentalism, relics, submission to the papal see—to England, and his haughty dealings with the older British church bred division, not unity.

expand to see more

The dictionary honours the genuine good in Augustine of Canterbury's mission. He obeyed the Great Commission, leaving Rome at Gregory's sending to carry the gospel to a heathen people, and under his preaching King Ethelbert and many of the men of Kent were baptized. That the name of Christ reached the Anglo-Saxons through his labour is a mercy of God, for how beautiful are the feet of them that bring glad tidings, and how shall a people believe without a preacher sent to them. The missionary impulse itself is to be commended wherever it is found.

Yet the dictionary will not idealize the mission or its fruit. The Christianity Augustine planted was the developing Roman religion, freighted with the sacramentalism, the veneration of relics and saints, and the submission to the papal see that the Reformation would later have to call the church away from. His dealings with the older Celtic British Christians, who had kept the faith in Britain long before him, were marked by a proud insistence on Roman usages and on submission to himself, breeding division rather than the unity of the Spirit. The dictionary applies its standing rule: honour the missionary zeal, name the Roman errors—the conversion of England was a real work of God, in a Roman dress that needed at last to be stripped away.

Hebrew Roots

Named for Augustine (Latin Augustinus, “venerable”); sent by Gregory the Great as a missionary, distinguished from the theologian Augustine of Hippo.

expand to see more

Augustinus, Latin, “venerable,” the name borne by both Augustines.

A Benedictine prior sent from Rome by Gregory the Great in 597.

First Archbishop of Canterbury, seat of the English church.

Distinguished sharply from Augustine of Hippo, the theologian of grace.

His mission planted the Roman, not the older Celtic, form of the faith.

Usage

"The teacher distinguished Augustine of Canterbury, the missionary, from Augustine of Hippo, the theologian."

"He honoured the zeal that brought Christ's name to the English, while naming the Roman errors it carried."

"She noted his proud dealings with the British church, which bred division rather than unity."
